meta.description: Not Aristotle. The line is absent from his works; its earliest known print source, Lowell L. Bennion’s 1959 book, credits it to Aristotle — but it matches nothing he wrote.

answer.label: Not Aristotle — and no verified author
answer.authorDates: Absent from Aristotle · earliest in print 1959 (Lowell L. Bennion, who credited Aristotle)
answer.sourceLine: Aristotle never wrote this; the sentence appears nowhere in his works. Its earliest documented print appearance is in the Latter-day Saint educator Lowell L. Bennion’s ‘Religion and the Pursuit of Truth’ (1959, p. 52), where Bennion set it in quotation marks and credited it to Aristotle — but it matches nothing in Aristotle’s texts, so whoever coined the wording, it is not authentic Aristotle.

author.name: Lowell L. Bennion
author.heading: About the real source
author.bio: Lowell Lindsay Bennion (1908–1996) was an American educator, sociologist and humanitarian who earned a doctorate in sociology at the University of Strasbourg and founded the Institute of Religion beside the University of Utah in 1934. His 1959 book Religion and the Pursuit of Truth — a rare Latter-day Saint work on epistemology — is the earliest known source of this famous line — but Bennion printed it in quotation marks and credited it to Aristotle, so whether he coined it or borrowed it is unknown. Either way, it matches nothing in Aristotle’s texts.

copyAttribution: "It is the mark of an educated mind to entertain a thought without accepting it" is routinely attributed to Aristotle, but he never wrote it. The line appears nowhere in his works; its earliest known print source is Lowell L. Bennion's "Religion and the Pursuit of Truth" (1959), p. 52, where he set it in quotation marks and credited it to Aristotle. Aristotle's genuine "mark of an educated man" line (Nicomachean Ethics I.3) is about matching precision to the subject.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most durable pseudo-Aristotle quotations. It has never been located in his writings.

items.why: Classicist Joel Christensen demonstrates the sentence is absent from Aristotle’s corpus ↗; the genuine ‘mark of an educated man’ line in Nicomachean Ethics I.3 is about precision, not entertaining ideas.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording first appears in Lowell L. Bennion’s 1959 book Religion and the Pursuit of Truth, p. 52 ↗ — where he credited it to Aristotle, though it matches nothing in his works.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: The counterfeit survives because it borrows Aristotle’s exact opening — “It is the mark of an educated…” — and then swaps in a wholly modern idea. Aristotle’s real sentence in the Nicomachean Ethics praises the educated person for demanding only as much precision as a subject allows; the popular version reassigns that same authority to open-minded skepticism, a distinctly 20th-century intellectual virtue.

Because the fake reads like something Aristotle should have said — and shares his cadence — it has become one of the most-shared ‘Aristotle’ lines online, printed on mugs, syllabi and LinkedIn posts, none of which can point to a passage.
detailsBody: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.3 (1094b, W. D. Ross translation): “It is the mark of an educated man to look for precision in each class of things just so far as the nature of the subject admits; it is evidently equally foolish to accept probable reasoning from a mathematician and to demand from a rhetorician scientific proofs.”
The subject there is method and expected rigor, not the psychological feat of holding an idea at arm’s length. The two sentences share a phrase and nothing else.
context.pull: The forgery keeps Aristotle’s first eight words and quietly replaces the rest.
